content: Whooping cough, also known as pertussis, is a highly contagious respiratory infection. Infants are particularly vulnerable to severe complications and even death from this disease. Currently, a 14-day course of erythromycin is recommended for both treatment of the infection and prophylaxis for individuals who have been in contact with infected persons. However, the effectiveness of this approach remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the risks and benefits of using antibiotics for treating whooping cough and for prophylaxis in both children and adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to January 2011. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that investigated antibiotic use for either treatment or prophylaxis of pertussis. A total of 13 trials involving 2,197 participants met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 11 trials examined treatment regimens, while two focused on prophylaxis. The quality of the trials varied. For eradicating Bordetella pertussis (the causative agent of whooping cough) from the nasopharynx, short-term antibiotic regimens (such as azithromycin for 3–5 days, or clarithromycin or erythromycin for 7 days) were found to be as effective as long-term regimens (erythromycin for 10–14 days). The risk ratio (RR) for effectiveness was 1.01 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.98 to 1.04). Importantly, short-term regimens were associated with fewer side effects compared to long-term regimens, with a risk ratio of 0.66 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.83). A 7-day course of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was also effective in eradicating the bacteria. There were no significant differences in clinical outcomes or rates of microbiological relapse between short-term and long-term antibiotic regimens. For prophylaxis in contacts older than six months of age, antibiotics did not significantly improve clinical symptoms or reduce the number of individuals who developed culture-positive B. pertussis. Side effects were reported with the use of antibiotics, and the type and frequency of these adverse effects varied depending on the specific antibiotic used. In conclusion, while antibiotics were effective in eliminating B. pertussis from the nasopharynx, they did not appear to influence the clinical progression of the disease. Additionally, there is insufficient evidence to determine the benefits of using antibiotics as a prophylactic measure for contacts of individuals with pertussis.
